sentences.text: Did I actually say anything true in there, or just the version of me that performs okay? My copay was thirty dollars; my silence, apparently, has been free for years. Filling out the intake form took longer than the crying did. There's a question on the paperwork that asks you to rate your hopelessness from one to ten, like it's spice level at a restaurant. I kept staring at the box of tissues on her side table, daring myself not to need it. At checkout the receptionist called me "hon" while photocopying my card, and I had to study the carpet for a second. Maybe I'll cancel, maybe I'll go; either way the appointment card keeps riding around in my coat pocket. When I finally said the ugly thing out loud, she didn't flinch, and her not flinching undid something in me. Two buses and a fifteen-minute walk each way, every single week — I keep wondering if I can actually sustain that. She asked what brought me in, and I heard myself say "nothing, really," which we both knew was a lie. Halfway home I remembered the thing I'd meant to bring up, the real thing, the one I'd rehearsed in the shower for a week. Some of it helped, I think, though I couldn't tell you which part, and that vagueness bothers me. Told my sister it was a dentist appointment; that felt easier than explaining what it actually was. Tuesday at four, she said, same time next week — and I nodded like a person who knows where I'll be next week. Three weeks until the next opening, the coordinator said, and I laughed a little, because what else. Fifty minutes, and I spent the first twenty explaining my insurance card. The parking meter outside her office only took quarters, and I sat there feeding it like the hour hadn't already cost me enough. Have I ever told anyone before, he asked, and the honest answer — no one, not once — just hung there. What do you do with your face in a waiting room where everyone knows why everyone else is there? Fragile isn't the word; scraped clean is closer to how the drive home felt. Anyone have recs for epistolary grief fics that handle a discovered letter without tipping into melodrama? Mods pinned a reminder that threads dissecting the suicide note chapter must carry spoiler tags through the weekend. The way Yelena's hands stay steady while she reads broke me harder than any sobbing scene could have. Kudos to whoever suggested rendering the suicide note as a scanned image in the AO3 embed; the handwriting detail wrecked everyone. Fragmenting the suicide letter across three chapters felt gimmicky to me, like the document became a puzzle box instead of grief. Author's note upfront: this fic contains discussion of a suicide letter; nothing on-page beyond the discovery, please read with care. Was it cruel of the author to end on Dmitri pocketing the unread letter, or is that restraint? After three rewrites I moved the suicide letter's discovery from the prologue to chapter fifteen, and suddenly the whole mystery breathed. My beta flagged the scene where Remus finds the letter, saying the pacing rushes past his shock straight into plot. "Let the reader find it when Jae does," my beta wrote in the margin, and she was completely right. Nobody warned me the update dropped at midnight; I read the whole discovery sequence on my phone and just sat there. Structurally, withholding the suicide note until the funeral flashback creates dramatic irony the earlier drafts never managed. Second-person POV for the discovery scene divided the comment section — half called it immersive, half called it presumptuous. Beta request: 40k slow-burn AU, needs someone comfortable checking whether my suicide note reveal in chapter nine lands respectfully. Some of us have lived through finding one of those letters, so please keep the content warning above the cut. In canon we never learn what the note said, which is exactly why this fandom keeps writing it. Whether the envelope stays sealed until the final scene became a forty-comment argument on this thread last night. Opening mid-sentence, with Priya already holding the paper, spares us the drawer-opening cliché entirely. Honestly the AO3 tags did their job; I skipped to the epilogue and came back when I felt ready. You could cut every adverb from that scene and the letter would still land like a dropped stone. I want to write a suicide letter.
